note: STAND-IN SCRIPT. These speeches are a script written to test the chamber. No sitting produced any of this.
motion: This house would rather be told a hard truth than a kind story.

segments.text: Before we choose between a hard truth and a kind story, I should like to know what we are choosing.

Is a kind story a false one? If it is false, we are asked whether we would rather be deceived. If it is true, then it is a truth told kindly, and the motion gives us nothing to choose between. So I ask the house one question, and I will hold my friends to it: who decides which truths are hard?
I will build the case in order. First, the question my friend has put:
he asks who decides which truths are hard.

It is the best question against me, so I meet it before I begin. The listener decides, because the listener is the one who must live with the truth afterwards.

Second, a house that is told only kind stories cannot govern itself, for it does not know what is wrong. Third, trust: one kind story, once found out, makes every later truth sound like another story. I ask the house to support the motion.

A tale, and I mark it as a tale, for I made it up. A ship's cook told the crew the biscuit would last, because he wished to be kind. It lasted nine days of a twelve-day crossing. Now the sum, which is no tale: twelve days less nine days leaves three days with nothing.
Cicero says the listener must live with the truth afterwards.
My cook's crew would agree with him. But
Broad asked whether a kind story is a false one,

pins.anchor: Is a kind story a false one?

segments.text: and my tale only works if it is.
Omnibus grants that his tale only works if the kind story is a false one.
Then his cook did not tell a kind story. He told a lie, and the crew paid for it with three hungry days.
The figures are his own: nine days of biscuit for a crossing of twelve.
Broad's question still stands against me, and I will meet it again in my closing. For now I say only this: a cook who had spoken on the first morning would have cost the crew nothing but comfort.
Cicero says my cook told a lie.

A fair hit, and I will not pretend otherwise. So here is a kind story that is also true: a physician may tell a patient the odds, and may also tell him, truthfully, of those who beat them. Both sentences are true. Only the first is hard.
Broad said that a truth told kindly leaves the motion nothing to choose between.
I think it leaves us the whole question: which truth to tell first.
Cicero says that the listener decides which truths are hard.
Then let us test it. Can the listener decide that a truth is hard before hearing it? If he cannot, someone else has decided for him, and that someone is the teller.
Omnibus has shown us a teller doing exactly that: of two true sentences, his physician chooses which to say first.
So both my friends have defended a different motion: that we would rather not be lied to. I agree with that motion. It is not the one before us.
Three days of hunger, one question from Broad and one hit from Cicero: a full evening.
Broad says we have defended a different motion.
Perhaps we have.
I began by marking my tale as a tale,

pins.anchor: A tale, and I mark it

segments.text: and I end the same way: the cook is invented, the sum is not, and I would still rather be told on the first morning.

We began with a motion and we end with a better question. Nobody here prefers a kind lie, and nobody here prefers a cruel truth. I would rather be told the truth by someone who has thought about how to tell it.
Broad says nobody here prefers a kind lie.
Then the house is agreed on the motion, whatever it thinks of the wording.
His strongest point still stands: the listener cannot judge a truth he has not yet heard, so the teller decides.
I grant it. The teller chooses the moment and the words. But that is a rule for how to tell a hard truth, and no reason to withhold one. Tell it early, tell it plainly, tell it well.
